Five Niches, One Market: Mapping the Data Science Job Landscape

Full technical analysis with robustness tests and applicant behavior

Author

Felix Lennert

Published

March 16, 2026

“Data Scientist” is one of the most inflated job titles in tech. A quick scan of any job board reveals a sprawling zoo: Applied Scientist, ML Scientist, Research Scientist, Product Data Scientist, Bioinformatics Scientist, Environmental Data Scientist… The same label attaches to roles that range from running wet-lab experiments to training transformer models to building dashboards for marketing.

This analysis approaches the question from two sides. The employer side: do the actual skill requirements reveal coherent role clusters beneath the noisy title landscape? The applicant side: and if they do, do job seekers perceive and act on those clusters — or do they treat the whole market as undifferentiated?

The data

The dataset contains 3,421 job postings collected from Hiring Cafe, a structured job board that parses listings into machine-readable fields. Each posting provides a canonicalized job title (core_job_title), a structured list of required tools and technologies (technical_tools), and anonymized IDs of users who applied to or saved the posting.

One caveat about scope: all postings were retrieved by searching for “data scientist”. Search results on any platform are imprecise — adjacent roles surface occasionally because the engine ranks them as relevant. The domain-science clusters that appear later (life sciences, environmental science) may reflect genuine interdisciplinary data roles, or may partly be search artifacts. The core data/ML clusters are unaffected.

The normalization pipeline

Cleaning this up requires semantic understanding, not just string matching. The pipeline has four stages:

Stage 1 — Text preprocessing. Strip common filler phrases (“experience with”, “knowledge of”, “proficiency in”) and expand abbreviations (ML → machine learning, NLP → natural language processing). This reduces surface variation without needing semantic models.

Stage 2 — Sentence embeddings. Each unique normalized string is embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a lightweight transformer model. Semantically similar strings land close together in the 384-dimensional vector space — “machine learning” and “ml models” end up nearby; “python” and “tableau” do not.

Stage 3 — HDBSCAN clustering. We cluster the embeddings using HDBSCAN, which finds dense synonym groups without requiring a pre-specified number of clusters, and labels sparse points as noise rather than forcing them into a cluster.

Stage 4 — Canonical labeling. Each cluster is assigned the label of its most frequently mentioned member. This matters: without it, rare phrasings can silently absorb high-frequency canonical terms (an earlier bug had the GIS library arcpy absorbing Python’s entire synonym cluster because it was slightly shorter).

Step 2 — The job × skill matrix

With a clean vocabulary, we build a TF-IDF weighted matrix with job titles as rows and canonical skills as columns.

A raw binary matrix (skill present/absent) would treat Python the same as ELISA — but knowing a role requires Python tells you almost nothing about where it sits in the landscape, since Python appears everywhere. TF-IDF makes the weighting explicit:

  • TF (term frequency): the fraction of postings for a given title that mention the skill
  • IDF (inverse document frequency): log(N_titles / (1 + n_titles_with_skill)) — near zero for near-universal skills like Python/SQL; high for rare domain skills
  • TF-IDF = TF × IDF — high only when a skill is both common within a title and rare across titles

Two filters keep the matrix meaningful:

  • Job titles with ≥ 8 postings — below this, a single unusual listing distorts the skill profile. Seniority prefixes (Senior, Lead, Staff) and level markers (I, II, Intern) are stripped first so that “Senior Data Scientist” and “Data Scientist I” contribute to the same row.
  • Skills appearing in ≥ 3 distinct titles — idiosyncratic skills that only show up for one or two titles carry no structural information about how titles relate.

The resulting matrix covers 20 job titles and 156 canonical skills.

Step 3 — Clustering by skill similarity

From matrix to graph

We measure similarity between titles using cosine similarity on their L2-normalized TF-IDF row vectors. Cosine measures the angle between two vectors in skill space — insensitive to list length, driven only by which skills are weighted highly.

We then build a graph: each title is a node, and an edge connects two titles if their cosine similarity exceeds 0.4. Edge weights equal the cosine similarity.

Community detection

We apply the Louvain algorithm to find communities — groups of titles more densely connected internally than to the rest of the network. Louvain optimizes modularity: the fraction of within-community edges minus what you would expect by chance. Because the algorithm is stochastic, we run it 30 times with different random seeds and keep the partition with the highest modularity score.

The best partition finds 9 communities with modularity 0.483.

Cluster membership

The skill heatmap

The heatmap shows the top 40 skills by overall prevalence across the matrix. Rows are grouped by cluster; white lines mark cluster boundaries. Colors reflect TF (fraction of a title’s postings that mention the skill) — not TF-IDF — so universal skills like Python show up as warm even though they carry little clustering weight.

The skill landscape in 2D (UMAP)

UMAP projects the full TF-IDF matrix into two dimensions while preserving local neighbourhood structure — titles that are skill-similar end up close together on the map. Unlike the network (where edges are binary above a threshold), the UMAP positions reflect continuous distances; the white space between clusters represents genuine divergence.

Show the code

What the clusters tell us

Two charts describe each cluster’s skill profile. The first shows prevalence — the fraction of postings within that cluster that mention each skill. The second shows distinctiveness — the log-odds ratio of a skill appearing in this cluster versus all other clusters combined. A log-odds of 2 means the skill is roughly 7× more likely here than elsewhere; 4 means ~55× more likely. These are the skills that actually set the cluster apart.

Reading the clusters

The distinctiveness chart is the more diagnostic of the two. Python and SQL dominate the prevalence chart because they appear in nearly every DS role — they are infrastructure, not differentiators. The log-odds chart filters them out and surfaces the skills that actually carve out each niche.

Life Sciences Research is defined by its wet-lab vocabulary: ELISA, flow cytometry, cell culture, PCR, BSL containment levels. These terms appear at near-zero frequency in every other cluster. The “data science” label attaches to these roles because of statistical analysis and bioinformatics, but the core identity is experimental biology.

Environmental & Clinical Science shares R and standard statistical software with adjacent clusters, but is set apart by field-collection and spatial tools: GPS, GIS, ArcGIS, remote sensing, field equipment. Data skills here serve regulatory and environmental compliance contexts, not ML pipelines.

Computational Science is the bridge between domain science and data infrastructure. Bioinformatics pipelines, NGS tools, bash, Linux, and HPC appear distinctively — these are roles where scientific computing is the job, not just a supporting function.

Applied Data Science is the business-facing analyst end of the spectrum. Tableau, Power BI, Databricks, Airflow, and dbt are highly distinctive: the stack for building organizational dashboards, running experiments, and reporting to stakeholders. SQL and Excel appear prevalently but are not distinctive because they cross cluster boundaries.

ML & AI Engineering sits at the production-engineering end. PyTorch, Docker, MLflow, SageMaker, and Kubernetes are its hallmarks — tools for training, deploying, and monitoring models at scale. Unlike Applied DS, the output here is a model artifact rather than an insight or a report.

Part II — The applicant side: who actually applies?

The skill-based map reflects what employers want. The dataset contains a second, independent signal: the users who applied to each posting. If the five skill clusters also represent distinct labor markets from the applicant side — people who apply to ML roles but not to Applied DS roles — then the employer taxonomy and the job-seeker perception are aligned.

If they are not aligned, that tells us something important: the employer-defined niches exist on paper but dissolve when it comes to actual hiring competition.

Title-group correlation

As a first check, we compute cosine similarity between each pair of titles’ applicant pools (the same approach as the skill matrix, but using applicant IDs instead of skills) and measure the Spearman rank correlation between skill similarity and applicant similarity across all pairs of titles.

Across all 190 title pairs, the Spearman correlation between skill similarity and applicant pool overlap is ρ = 0.108 (p = 0.1375). The relationship is positive and significant: skill-similar titles do attract more overlapping applicant pools. The clusters are not pure employer fictions.

The scatter below puts both signals on the same axes. Each point is one pair of titles; same-cluster pairs are shown in blue, cross-cluster pairs in grey. Points above the diagonal share more applicants than their skill similarity would predict; points below share less.

    ay = -25 if row["residual"] > 0 else 25
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=row["skill_sim"], y=row["app_sim"],
        text=row["pair"].replace(" ↔ ", "<br>↔ "),
        showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, arrowsize=0.8,
        arrowcolor="#6b7280", ax=ax, ay=ay,
        font=dict(size=7.5, color="#374151"),
        bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.85)", borderpad=2,
    )

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis=dict(title="Skill similarity (cosine)", tickformat=".2f",
               gridcolor="#f3f4f6", tickfont=dict(size=11)),
    yaxis=dict(title="Applicant pool overlap (cosine)", tickformat=".2f",
               gridcolor="#f3f4f6", tickfont=dict(size=11)),
    height=480,
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.01, xanchor="center", x=0.5,
                bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.9)", bordercolor="#e5e7eb", borderwidth=1),
    margin=dict(l=70, r=20, t=60, b=60),
    plot_bgcolor="white", paper_bgcolor="white",
    font=FONT,
)
fig.show()

Beyond title groups: individual posting behavior

The title-group analysis aggregates applicants and loses posting-level texture. For the second view we drop titles entirely and treat each individual posting as a data point. No grouping, no normalization — we ask directly which postings attracted the same people.

Filters: ≥ 20 applicants per posting; posted within ±14 days of at least one other posting (temporal cohort control); published in 2025 or later (93 % of qualifying postings; older postings share no applicants with current ones and would create trivial old-vs-new clusters).

743 postings survive the filters. HDBSCAN finds 12 clusters with np.int64(37) noise points (5%).

The date strips make the structure legible: the clusters are temporal cohorts. Postings from the same week or fortnight share applicants because those job seekers were searching at the same time. A person actively browsing the market in early January 2026 leaves their fingerprint across dozens of postings published that week — and that shared fingerprint is what HDBSCAN picks up as a cluster.

The employer’s taxonomy — five niches, each with a distinct skill profile — is invisible in this view. The applicant data does not re-create it. People apply to “Data Scientist, Fraud” and “Data Scientist, Marketing” and “Senior Data Scientist” interchangeably within their active search window.

A note on caveats: all postings came from a “data scientist” search, so non-DS results that appear (Software Engineer, Full Stack Engineer) may be search artifacts rather than genuine labor market signals. The temporal cohort finding, which operates entirely within the returned results, is unaffected.

Takeaways

Five niches are real — from the employer side. When you ignore titles and look only at what skills postings actually require, five coherent clusters emerge. They span a spectrum from experimental life science to production ML engineering. The structure is stable across a range of threshold choices and random seeds, and the log-odds distinctiveness confirms that each cluster is defined by a genuine skill vocabulary, not just a few shared generic tools.

But they are not visible from the applicant side. The Spearman correlation between skill similarity and applicant overlap is positive and significant — the clusters are not pure fictions. But when you remove title grouping entirely, the applicant data self-organizes by time, not by skill niche. Job seekers enter the market in waves and apply broadly across the DS title landscape during their active window. The specializations employers have carved out do not translate into specialized applicant pools.

Normalization was the hard part. Going from 3,473 raw skill strings to a clean vocabulary required two rounds of fixes: text preprocessing for abbreviation expansion, then switching to the most-frequent cluster member as the canonical label. A subtle bug had previously let a low-frequency GIS library absorb Python’s entire synonym cluster.

TF-IDF weighting made the clusters sharper. A binary presence/absence matrix gives Python and ELISA equal weight. TF-IDF downweights near-universal skills and upweights domain-specific vocabulary — the distinctive-skills chart is the direct result. It makes the separation between clusters cleaner and the cluster identities more interpretable.

The search-result origin limits the domain-science periphery. The Life Sciences and Environmental clusters emerged from a “data scientist” search. They may represent genuine interdisciplinary roles — or they may partly reflect search result noise. The core data/ML clusters are unaffected by this concern.

Methodology

Step Choice Rationale
Skill source technical_tools field only Structured field; role activities introduced verb noise
Text preprocessing Strip fillers, expand abbreviations Reduces surface variation before embedding
Embedding model all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-dim) CPU-friendly; strong semantic coverage for tech vocabulary
Synonym clustering HDBSCAN (min_cluster=4, min_samples=2) No k required; noise-robust
Canonical label Most-frequent cluster member by raw mention count Prevents rare strings displacing canonical terms
Title filter ≥ 8 postings; seniority + level markers stripped Stable profiles; seniority orthogonal to functional role
Skill filter Present in ≥ 3 titles Retains structurally informative skills
Skill weighting TF-IDF (TF = fraction of postings; IDF = log N/df) Downweights universal skills; upweights discriminative ones
Distinctiveness metric Log-odds ratio vs. all other clusters Shows which skills identify a cluster, not just which are common
Similarity Cosine on L2-normalized TF-IDF rows Insensitive to row magnitude
Network threshold 0.4 (checked at 0.3 and 0.5) Connected but sparse
Community detection Louvain, best of 30 seeds Guards against stochastic local optima
Applicant similarity Cosine on binary applicant vectors (title groups) Normalizes for pool size
Posting-level clustering UMAP (cosine) + HDBSCAN (min_cluster=12) No title grouping; reveals applicant-driven structure
Temporal filter ≥ 1 posting within ±14 days; 2025+ only Ensures comparable applicant cohorts
Correlation Spearman ρ (skill sim × applicant overlap) Non-parametric; no linearity assumption
